stage1.probe_response:
Summary of what the sensors show
- The blade is encountering a geometric interlock with the grill ribs plus adhesive friction from the sticky residue, not just plain surface sliding.
- Evidence:
  - The grill has deep, regularly spaced gaps (ribs running along X) so a flat blade placed straight across spans many rib tops.
  - Even a light straight probe produced a substantial lateral force (85 N) and a downward deflection into the gaps (z = −0.02 m).
  - Increasing the push to 150 N barely increased forward displacement (0.015 → 0.017 m) while structural stress rose to ~148 N/m^2 and material_strain ≈ 0.94 (near-failure/large strain). That says the blade is jammed/loaded, not simply overcoming low friction.

Why simply increasing Y-axis force won't work
- Geometry: the blade edge is catching the front faces/edges of the raised ribs. To move forward the blade must either climb up over the rib tops or be guided into the gap; a pure forward (Y) force produces no lifting moment to get the blade over the ribs. Instead the forward force is reacted by the ribs as a vertical/wedging reaction, so the blade is pushed further into the gaps (increased z deflection) and the structure takes higher stress.
- Adhesion + friction: the residue adds a high shear/friction component along the contact points, so more Y force primarily increases contact stress rather than enabling forward motion.
- Risk/ineffectiveness: pushing harder just raises stress and strain (we are already near material strain limits) and risks damage or permanent jamming. It does not change the contact geometry that prevents forward motion.

Implication: to clear the residue you must change the contact geometry (e.g., add lift or rotation to ride over ribs, align the blade with the gaps, or apply a scraping motion that includes a normal/rotational component), not just increase the pure Y-axis push.

tool_selection.full_response:
(1) Guiding physical principle
- Scraping performance is set by the balance of lateral shear force (to overcome the adhesive/frictional bond of the residue) and the normal force/geometry that keeps the blade riding on the raised bars rather than falling into gaps. In practice that means: (a) supply lateral force greater than the measured steady lateral resistance, (b) keep a controlled normal force and a slight forward pitch so the blade's leading edge stays on the raised surfaces and does not plunge into gaps, and (c) use a moderate scraping speed to avoid shock-loading the blade/material.

(2) How the probe data confirms the problem
- PROBE_STRAIGHT: lateral force ~85 N at low probe — the residue presents significant friction even at light push. The blade also displaced downward z = -0.020 m, showing the edge can fall into the grill gaps under light contact.
- PROBE_HARD_STRAIGHT: commanded lateral force 150 N was transmitted (force_y = 150 N) and material_strain = 0.94 (near yielding), indicating we reached near the material resistance threshold but still saw significant strain and stress. The higher force did not eliminate the z-drop tendency in the earlier probe and suggests that a single pass will require a force safely above 150 N to reliably shear the sticky residue across the whole width.

(3) Physical reasoning for chosen numeric parameters
- Lateral applied_force.y = 200.0 N: PROBE_HARD_STRAIGHT at 150 N produced near-yield strain (0.94). To ensure a single continuous scrape across the width, choose a margin above that observed resistance. 200 N provides ~33% margin over the 150 N test to overcome variations and adhesion without being excessively large.
- Applied_force.z = -50.0 N (downward normal): the initial probe showed the blade dropping into gaps; to keep the blade riding on the raised bars we must apply a controlled downward normal so the blade seats on the ridges rather than slipping into grooves. A moderate downward preload (~50 N) will press the blade onto the ridges but not so large as to risk damaging the grill or tool.
- Orientation pitch = 5.0 degrees (leading edge slightly downward): a small forward pitch ensures the leading edge contacts the raised cooking bars first and stably shears residue; it reduces the tendency of the blade to catch on the side of a bar and to wedge into a gap.
- Linear_velocity.y = 0.03 m/s: a modest scraping speed is chosen so the high lateral force is applied steadily (reducing shock and chatter) and sensor feedback is still relevant; faster motion risks sudden impacts or dynamic bouncing into gaps.

stage3.probe_response:
Short answer: Partially. The sensing and grasping steps succeeded and gave the right physical insight, but the single continuous forward-scrape plan failed repeatedly because the scraper was not oriented to span the grill gaps (effective contact width was only 0.005 m) and the arm/base approach prevented laying the blade across the bars. I would change the sequence and some parameters next time to avoid trying one high‑force pass while the blade is aligned with the push direction.

What succeeded
- Navigation to the countertop/grill (initial NAVIGATE_TO with the proper available args) and visual/geometry inspection of the grill and scraper — I obtained the surface topology and tool geometry needed to plan.
- PROBE_STRAIGHT and PROBE_HARD_STRAIGHT executed and produced useful force/displacement/strain data that revealed high lateral resistance (~85 N at light probe, ~150 N near-yield at hard probe) and that the blade tended to drop into the gaps (z drop ≈ -0.02 m).
- GRASP and RELEASE of the scraper were successful when used.

What failed and why
- The main cleaning action(s) failed:
  - The first PUSH_FORWARD (planned with 200 N lateral, -50 N preload, 5° pitch) failed because the blade dropped into the gaps and the profile in the push direction was too narrow to bridge the bars.
  - Repeated NEW_ACTION PLACE/PUSH attempts failed because the manipulator kept presenting the blade aligned with the push direction (so effective cleaning width remained 0.005 m versus grill width 0.2 m). In short: the tool orientation relative to the grill was wrong, so a single forward scrape could not contact the full surface.
  - Some PLACE_ON_TOP attempts returned “No forward push motion detected,” indicating the command semantics or parameters were not matched to the desired combined placement+scrape behavior.
  - NAVIGATE_TO usage later produced a TypeError — that indicates I tried a navigation primitive with incorrect arguments (argument/API mismatch) while trying to change the base/arm approach.

Root causes
- Mechanical: The blade geometry in the current grasp/orientation did not bridge the grill gaps when pushed forward (it needed to be rotated ~90° yaw so the blade spans across the bars). With the blade aligned along the push axis it simply fell into grooves or contacted only a narrow edge.
- Strategy: I committed to a single high-force pass before ensuring the blade was laid across the grill and seated on the front lip.
- Execution/API: Attempts to combine place-and-scrape or to reposition via NAVIGATE used command variants that were either unsupported or mis-specified, which produced errors or unintended behavior.

How I would approach it next time (concrete changes and why)
1. Verify and set tool yaw to span the grill before applying lateral force
   - Explicitly rotate the tool so the blade is perpendicular to the push direction (yaw ≈ 90°) and confirm the robot reports the scraper’s effective cleaning width ≈ grill width. This avoids plunging into gaps.
   - Rationale: bridging the bars is required to keep the blade riding on raised surfaces.

2. Reposition base/arm for a side/top approach if the current pose prevents laying the blade across
   - Move the base or change the arm approach early (with correct NAVIGATE_TO syntax / supported primitives) so the wrist can orient the scraper to span the grill.
   - Rationale: repeated failed place attempts indicated the current approach geometry prevented the required yaw/pitch configuration.

3. Place the scraper on the front lip (seat it) before the scrape
   - Perform a deliberate PLACE (blade across grill, slight forward offset, small downward preload) to seat the blade on the ridges, then do a separate PUSH_FORWARD stroke.
   - Rationale: separating placement and push reduces command complexity and lets me confirm full-width contact before applying high lateral force.

4. Use incremental force ramps and multiple passes rather than one very large stroke
   - Start scraping at a safe lateral force slightly above the measured steady force (e.g., 160–180 N) with a downward preload to stay on ridges; if residue remains, increase force or do several overlapping passes across the width.
   - Rationale: PROBE_HARD_STRAIGHT showed 150 N reached near-yield; using a margin is OK but multiple controlled passes reduce the chance of wedging or tool blockage and reduce damage risk.

5. Use a small forward pitch and steady, modest velocity
   - Keep leading-edge pitch (≈ 3–7°) and slow velocity (~0.02–0.04 m/s) as planned to keep the blade contacting raised bars without shock loads.
   - Rationale: keeps edge on ridges and reduces bouncing into gaps.

6. Validate tool effective width/pose before pushing
   - Query an explicit status (effective cleaning width or contact footprint) after placing to ensure the blade will cover the full grill; if not, adjust orientation/pose.
   - Rationale: would have detected the 0.005 m effective width earlier and prevented repeated failed pushes.

7. If single-pass still infeasible, switch scraping direction or use sweeping motions
   - Either do multiple adjacent passes while incrementally translating the blade sideways, or rotate the workpiece orientation (if possible) to let the blade sweep along a direction where it naturally bridges the gaps.
   - Rationale: flexibility in stroke direction can avoid geometric constraints.

8. Fix command/API usage
   - Before attempting more complex base/arm moves, verify and use the correct NAVIGATE_TO and placement primitives and parameter formats to avoid TypeError and “No forward push motion detected” issues.
   - Rationale: avoid wasted attempts caused by incorrect primitive calls.

Summary
- The sensing and manipulation primitives gave correct diagnosis (too much lateral resistance; blade falls into gaps). The plan failed because I attempted a single high-force forward scrape while the scraper was not oriented to span the grill gaps and the approach pose prevented laying it across the bars. Next time I would first ensure the blade is laid across and seated on the front lip (or reposition the base/arm to allow that), confirm full-width contact, then perform controlled scraping with incremental force and multiple passes as needed.
